content: # Derivatives of Vectors and Vector-valued Functions

label: text
content: Mathematics is a collection of cheap tricks and dirty jokes. Lipman Bers

label: text
content: Quantitative genetics often deals with vector-valued functions, and here we provide a brief review of the calculus of such functions. In particular, we review common expressions for derivatives of vectors and vector-valued functions, introduce the gradient vector and Hessian matrix (for first and second partials, respectively), and use this machinery in multidimensional Taylor series for approximating functions around a specific value. We apply these results to several problems in selection theory and evolution.

label: text
content: ## DERIVATIVES OF VECTORS AND VECTOR-VALUED FUNCTIONS

label: text
content: Suppose we let $ f(\mathbf{x}) $ be a scalar (single-dimension) function of a column vector, $ \mathbf{x}= ( x_{1},\cdots,x_{n} )^{T} $ of n variables. The gradient (or gradient vector) of f with respect to x is obtained by taking partial derivatives of the function with respect to each variable. In matrix notation, the gradient operator is denoted by

label: formula
content:
$$
\nabla_ {\mathbf {X}} [ f ] = \frac {\partial f}{\partial \mathbf {x}} = \left( \begin{array}{c} \frac {\partial f}{\partial x _ {1}} \\ \vdots \\ \frac {\partial f}{\partial x _ {n}} \end{array} \right)
$$

label: text
content: The gradient at a point, $ \mathbf{x}_{o} $ , corresponds to a vector indicating the direction of local steepest ascent of the function at that point (the multivariate slope of f at $ \mathbf{x}_{o} $ ).

content: ## THE HESSIAN MATRIX, LOCAL MAXIMA/MINIMA, AND MULTIDIMENSIONAL TAYLOR SERIES

label: text
content: In univariate calculus, the local extrema of a function occur when its slope (first derivative) is zero. The multivariate extension is that the gradient vector is zero, so the slope of the function with respect to all variables is zero. A point $ x_{e} $ where this occurs is called a stationary or equilibrium point, and corresponds to either a local maximum, minimum, saddle point, or inflection point. As with the calculus of single variables, determining which of these cases is correct depends on the second derivative. With n variables, the appropriate generalization is the Hessian matrix

label: formula
content:
$$
\mathbf {H} _ {\mathbf {X}} [ f ] = \nabla_ {\mathbf {X}} \left[ \left(\nabla_ {\mathbf {X}} [ f ]\right) ^ {T} \right] = \frac {\partial^ {2} f}{\partial \mathbf {x} \partial \mathbf {x} ^ {T}} = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} \frac {\partial^ {2} f}{\partial x _ {1} ^ {2}} & \dots & \frac {\partial^ {2} f}{\partial x _ {1} \partial x _ {n}} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \frac {\partial^ {2} f}{\partial x _ {1} \partial x _ {n}} & \dots & \frac {\partial^ {2} f}{\partial x _ {n} ^ {2}} \end{array} \right)
$$

label: text
content: Note that this is the outer product of $ \nabla_{\mathbf{X}}[f] $ with itself. Recall for an n-dimensional column vector $ \mathbf{a}_{n\times 1} $ that while the inner product, $ \mathbf{a}_{1\times n}^{T}\mathbf{a}_{n\times 1}=\sum a_{i} $ returns a $ 1\times 1 $ matrix (a scalar), the outer product, $ \mathbf{a}_{n\times 1}\mathbf{a}_{1\times n}^{T} $ returns an $ n\times n $ matrix whose ijth element is $ a_{i}a_{j} $ or (in our case)

label: formula
text
content: This matrix is symmetric, as mixed partials are equal under suitable continuity conditions, and it measures the local multidimensional curvature of the function.

Consider the (second-order) Taylor series of a scalar function of n variables, $ f ( x_{1}, \dots, x_{n} ) $ , expanded about the point $ \mathbf{x}_{o} $

label: text
content: Occasionally, we wish to find the maximum or minimum of a function subject to a constraint. The solution is to use Lagrange multipliers. Suppose we wish to find the extrema of a function, f(x), subject to the constraint that $ h(\mathbf{x})=c $ . We first construct a new function by considering

label: formula
content:
$$
g (\mathbf {x}, \lambda) = f (\mathbf {x}) - \lambda [ h (\mathbf {x}) - c ]
$$

label: text
content: Because $ h (\mathbf{x})-c=0 $ , the extrema of $ g (\mathbf{x},\lambda) $ correspond to the extrema of $ f (\mathbf{x}) $ under the constraint. Local maxima and minima are obtained by solving the following set of equations:

label: formula
content:
$$

abla_ {\mathbf {X}} [ g (\mathbf {x}, \lambda) ] = 
abla_ {\mathbf {X}} [ f (\mathbf {x}) ] - \lambda \cdot 
abla_ {\mathbf {X}} [ h (\mathbf {x}) ] = 0
$$

label: formula
content:
$$
\frac {d g (\mathbf {x} , \lambda)}{d \lambda} = h (\mathbf {x}) - c = 0
$$

label: text
content: Observe that the second equation is satisfied by the constraint.
